meta.title: K-12 funding, teachers and TEA, 17 days of posts
meta.subject: K-12 public education funding and the teaching profession in Texas — school finance and the basic allotment, teacher pay and retention, certification and alternative certification including Teach for America, the TEA budget and its riders, academic competition funding, A-F accountability ratings, and school district budget deficits
meta.subtitle: Oct 1 to Oct 17, 2026. Each dot is one post with 1K+ views about Texas K-12 funding, teachers and TEA, plus every post repeating an earlier one, in the lane for what it argues. Higher and bigger means more views. White means 90% or more the same words as an earlier post, with a white line back to it. Coloured lines link a post to the post it quoted or replied to. Updated daily.

lanes.label: Texas teacher pay lags, exodus
lanes.description: Texas pays teachers too little (ranked around 31st-33rd nationally), driving burnout, attrition and shortages, and teachers deserve better compensation and respect.

lanes.label: Vouchers drain public school funds
lanes.description: Texas's voucher/ESA program pulls students and dollars from public schools, leaving districts with lost funding, deficits and closures.

lanes.label: Fix schools at the ballot box
lanes.description: Underfunded schools and poor teacher pay are blamed on Republican leaders like Abbott and Paxton, and voters are urged to back Democrats such as Talarico and Hinojosa.

lanes.label: District deficits are mismanagement
lanes.description: District budget deficits stem from wasteful spending and poor management, not too little state money, and call for audits and transparency such as the Comptroller's reviews.

lanes.label: Certification, TEA and accountability
lanes.description: Debates over alternative certification, uncertified hires, Teach for America, A-F ratings and TEA's takeover and oversight powers, framed as either lowering standards or enabling accountability and flexibility.

lanes.label: State underfunds schools, basic allotment
lanes.description: The Legislature's basic allotment and school finance choices fail to keep up with inflation, forcing districts into cuts, so more state funding is needed.

lanes.label: Pushback
lanes.description: Posts doubting, mocking, fact-checking or arguing against the dominant framings.

posts.name: Caring Guy💙🇺🇸🌈✌🏻
posts.text:
@realBrandonGill I get it, you're scared, so you lie.

Calling James Talarico a “weirdo” is an opinion, from a weirdo. But if you’re going to build your argument around his record versus Ken Paxton’s, at least get the facts right.

First, Talarico never said there are “six genders.” In a 2021 Texas House hearing, he said there were six biological sexes while discussing chromosomal variations and intersex conditions. That was an imprecise statement, and he has since publicly corrected it, saying there are two sexes and a small percentage of people with genetic variations.

Yes, Talarico said “God is nonbinary.” But the context matters. He was making a theological argument that God transcends human sex, not claiming God is transgender. That concept is hardly some bizarre invention. Even the Catholic Catechism says God “is neither man nor woman.” Talarico has explained his position by pointing to Galatians and the traditional Christian idea that God is not biologically male or female.

Now, since you want to compare records, James Talarico is a former public-school teacher who has served in the Texas House since 2018. Among the legislation he has worked on or helped pass:

• Helped write Texas’ major 2019 school-finance overhaul, which increased public-school funding and teacher compensation.
• Sponsored the law establishing Texas’ first statewide cap on pre-K class sizes.
• Worked on legislation capping insulin copays at $25 for a 30-day supply.
• Passed legislation expanding student mental-health and character-education programs.
• Worked to improve child-care affordability and quality.
• Passed legislation expanding educational opportunities for incarcerated young people who had not completed high school.
• Authored legislation expanding access to school-safety and active-shooter training.
• Worked on legislation addressing fentanyl overdoses and access to opioid-reversal medication in schools.

The Texas House itself credits him with those accomplishments, and the Texas Tribune reports that 16 bills he led have become law, half of them involving education, child care, or youth workforce development.

Now let’s look at Ken Paxton.

Paxton was indicted in 2015 on three felony securities charges involving allegations that he solicited investors without disclosing that he was being compensated and acted as an unregistered investment adviser. He avoided trial through a pretrial-diversion agreement requiring him to pay $271,000 in restitution, perform more than 100 hours of community service, and complete ethics training. The charges were formally dismissed in June 2025 after he completed those requirements.

Then there were the allegations from senior employees in his own attorney general’s office that he abused his office to benefit wealthy donor Nate Paul. The Republican-controlled Texas House investigated those allegations and impeached Paxton in 2023 on charges including bribery and abuse of office. A federal corruption investigation also ended without charges when the Justice Department declined prosecution. 

But the whistleblowers’ civil case did not disappear. In 2025, a Texas judge found by a preponderance of the evidence that Paxton’s office violated the state whistleblower law by retaliating against four former senior employees who reported him to the FBI. The judgment totaled $6.6 million, and Paxton subsequently dropped the state’s appeal.

Paxton’s wife, Republican state Sen. Angela Paxton, also filed for divorce in 2025 and specifically alleged adultery. Allegations of an extramarital affair had previously played a role in the impeachment investigation. Those are allegations, not criminal convictions.

Paxton has taken more than 275 out-of-state trips while attorney general, left roughly 730 workdays blank on his official calendars, and incurred at least $1.9 million in taxpayer-funded security costs during his tenure.

Your claim that he “sued 130 cities” over property taxes is a lie. His office sent violation letters to more than 130 municipalities after determining they had failed to comply with financial-audit requirements established by a 2025 Texas law. The letters told those cities they could not raise property-tax rates above the no-new-revenue rate. That is not the same thing as filing 130 lawsuits.

So there certainly is a clear contrast. Talarico’s record includes years as a public-school teacher and legislation involving education, insulin costs, child care, school safety, juvenile education, and drug-overdose prevention. Paxton’s record includes significant legal settlements for Texas, but also a felony indictment resolved through restitution, community service, and ethics training, impeachment by the Texas House, a multimillion-dollar whistleblower judgment against his office, allegations of adultery from his wife, and years of investigations and litigation surrounding his conduct in office.

That is the actual record. You don’t need to invent “six genders” or 130 lawsuits to compare them.

posts.text:
BREAKING: The State of Texas is opening the books on Austin ISD.

Texas Comptroller Don Huffines picked Austin ISD as one of four districts for a top to bottom review of how it spent your tax dollars last school year. Austin ISD's projected deficit ballooned from $19.5 million to $105 million, and the state already dropped its financial rating to a B, the first time in 21 years it missed the top mark.

If the state thinks Austin needs an outside look, Round Rock families deserve one too. Before Round Rock ISD gets another dime, we need a forensic audit.

Vote NO on RRISD Prop A. Early voting runs Oct. 19–30.

Theodore Schramm, Texas House District 136 | https://t.co/CdWRrAeVsY
#TX136 #RoundRocktx #RRISD #AISD #Austintx #TXLege

posts.text: @esjesjesj This is common, although I wouldn’t complain if a teacher didn’t provide their contact info because they aren’t on call 24/7.  Texas ranks 33rd for public school teacher pay. A teacher’s availability to assist outside of normal hours is a value-added feature, not a “creepy” bug.
